Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** supplies an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$ and the absolute-time coordinate. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A **material motion** is a map $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ such that each $\chi_t=\chi(t,\cdot)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open image, has a $C^2$ inverse, and has positive Jacobian determinant; in the initial chart set $\chi(0,a)=a$. The label $a\in U$ and position $x=\chi(t,a)$ are measured in metres. Write

$$F(t,a)=D_a\chi(t,a),\qquad J(t,a)=\det F(t,a)>0,\qquad A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x),\qquad \Omega_t=\chi_t(B).$$

before.quote:
Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Use a smooth single-component, nonpolar fluid branch in a Cartesian inertial frame. Let $\mathcal U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be an open state domain with coordinates $v$ and $s$, where $v$ is specific volume and $s$ is specific entropy. Adopt a specific internal-energy function $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$, meaning that its coordinate partial derivatives through total order two exist and are continuous. At a state $(v,s)$, define the temperature and thermodynamic pressure by
$$ T(v,s)=\frac{\partial e}{\partial s}(v,s),\qquad p(v,s)=-\frac{\partial e}{\partial v}(v,s),\qquad \rho=\frac1v, $$
where each partial derivative holds the other state coordinate fixed. Assume the local material states lie in $\mathcal U$ and $T>0$. Local equilibrium here means that the fields $e,T,p$ at each event are assigned by these state functions of the local $v,s$.

In the physical SI interpretation, $v$ is in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $e$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, and $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. Positivity of $e_{ss}$, global invertibility of $s\mapsto T$, convexity, and the dynamical entropy inequality are separate assumptions or postulates; none follows from this local equilibrium adoption. This closure is an additional physical model choice, not a consequence of global equilibrium thermodynamics.

Use a Cartesian inertial frame in Newtonian spacetime. At an event let $u$ be the fluid velocity, $T>0$ its temperature, $\rho>0$ its mass density, and $\xi=(\rho,T)$ its local state in a specified open set $\mathcal S\subset(0,\infty)^2$. The velocity gradient has components $L_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$; define the symmetric rate matrix $D=(L+L^T)/2$, its trace $\theta=\operatorname{tr}D$, and its trace-free part $D_0=D-\theta I_3/3$, where $I_3$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. For $A,B\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, use the Frobenius contraction $A:B=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Assume it is real-linear, meaning $\mathcal A_\xi(aD+bE)=a\mathcal A_\xi(D)+b\mathcal A_\xi(E)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $D,E\in\operatorname{Sym}(3)$, and equivariant in the sense $\mathcal A_\xi(QDQ^T)=Q\mathcal A_\xi(D)Q^T$ for every $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$. Adopt
$$ \tau=\mathcal A_\xi(D)=2\mu(\xi)D_0+\zeta(\xi)\theta I_3,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+\tau,\qquad q=-K(\xi)\nabla T. $$
Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets has a function $f$ with $f(n)\in X_n$ for every $n$. Let $U\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be open and let $e:U\to\mathbb R$ have continuous total derivatives through order two. For $(v,s)\in U$, $v$ is the specific-volume coordinate, $s$ the specific-entropy coordinate, and $e(v,s)$ the specific-energy value; set $T=e_s(v,s)$ and $p=-e_v(v,s)$, with each state partial derivative holding the other coordinate fixed.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval. Let $B\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set with $C^1$ boundary, meaning that near every boundary point it is the graph of a continuously differentiable function after a rigid coordinate change. Let $N\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subset N$, and let $\chi\in C^2(I\times N,\mathbb R^3)$, where $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. For each $t\in I$, assume $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is a bijection from $N$ onto an open set with a $C^2$ inverse and $\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$. Define $\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$, $\Omega:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$, and $u(t,x):=\partial_t\chi(t,\chi_t^{-1}(x))$; this swept set $\Omega$ is open. For a scalar or vector field $f$ on $\Omega$, set $D_tf:=\partial_tf+\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}f$ componentwise. For each nonempty bounded open $C^1$ subdomain $V$ with $\overline V\subset B$, set $P_t:=\chi_t(V)$; here a $C^1$ domain is locally on one side of a $C^1$ boundary graph.

Let $\rho,v,s,T,p,q,r,b$ be fields on $\Omega$ with continuous first partial derivatives, with $\rho>0$, $(v,s)\in U$, $v=1/\rho$, $T=e_s(v,s)>0$, and $p=-e_v(v,s)$. Let $e$ on $\Omega$ denote the composition $e(v,s)$. Let $\sigma$ be a continuously differentiable $3\times3$ stress matrix field, let $\tau$ be a continuously differentiable $3\times3$ matrix field, and suppose $\sigma=-pI+\tau$, where $I$ is the $3\times3$ identity. For a scalar field $h$, define $(\nabla h)_i:=\partial_{x_i}h$; define $L:=\nabla u$ by $L_{ij}:=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D:=(L+L^T)/2$, and $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$. Define $A:B:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$ for matrices, $\operatorname{div}q:=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}q_i$, and $\operatorname{div}(q/T)$ componentwise. Put $a_m:=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, $k:=|u|^2/2$, and $E:=e+k$. The fields $u,q,b$ are vector-valued and $r$ is scalar-valued.

Assume there is a contact traction $t_c(t,y,n)\in\mathbb R^3$ depending on a surface only through its point $y$ and outward unit normal $n\in S^2$, continuous in $(y,n)$ and uniformly bounded near each point. For a scalar field $h$, define $(\nabla h)_i:=\partial_{x_i}h$; define $L:=\nabla u$ by $L_{ij}:=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D:=(L+L^T)/2$, and $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}D=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$. Define $A:B:=\sum_{i,j=1}^3A_{ij}B_{ij}$ for matrices, $\operatorname{div}q:=\sum_i\partial_{x_i}q_i$, and $\operatorname{div}(q/T)$ componentwise. Put $a_m:=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, $k:=|u|^2/2$, and $E:=e+k$. The fields $u,q,b$ are vector-valued and $r$ is scalar-valued.

Assume there is a contact traction $t_c(t,y,n)\in\mathbb R^3$ depending on a surface only through its point $y$ and outward unit normal $n\in S^2$, continuous in $(y,n)$ and uniformly bounded near each point. Assume its local force balance $\int_{\partial P}t_c(t,y,\nu_P(y))\,dS_y+\int_P\rho(t,y)(b(t,y)-a_m(t,y))\,dy=0$ for every nonempty bounded open $C^1$ subdomain $P$ whose closure is compactly contained in $\Omega_t$. Surface integrals use Euclidean surface measure with chart area density $\sqrt{\det(DX^TDX)}$. Suppose the unique Cauchy stress supplied by this contact balance satisfies $t_c(t,y,n)=\sigma(t,y)n$ and has the stated $C^1$ regularity; the contact result alone does not imply that regularity.

Assume the pointwise continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ and, for every such material subdomain $V$ and every $t\in I$, the integral balances
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\sigma\nu\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times(\sigma\nu)\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho E\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}(\sigma\nu)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial P_t}q\cdot\nu\,dS+\int_{P_t}\rho r\,dx,$$
where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal, $\times$ is the ordinary vector cross product, and all fields are continuous up to the swept closures. The angular-momentum balance gives $\sigma=\sigma^T$, and the local internal-energy equation supplied by these hypotheses is $\rho D_te=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}q+\rho r$. Define the entropy residual $\mathcal G:=\rho D_ts+\operatorname{div}(q/T)-\rho r/T$. Then
$$\mathcal G=\frac{\tau:D}{T}-\frac{q\cdot\nabla T}{T^2}.$$
At any state with $e_{ss}>0$, a unique local $C^1$ branch $s(v,T)$ satisfies $e_s(v,s(v,T))=T$; the local Helmholtz function $a(v,T):=e(v,s(v,T))-Ts(v,T)$ then satisfies $a_T=-s$ and $a_v=-p$. The entropy identity does not assert $\mathcal G\ge0$ and makes no empirical claim. In the physical SI interpretation, $\rho$ is in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $b$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $v$ in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}}$, $e,k,E$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$, $s$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $T$ in $\mathrm K$, $p,\sigma,\tau,t_c$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $r$ in $\mathrm{W\,kg^{-1}}$.

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** supplies an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$ and the absolute-time coordinate. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference body whose boundary is locally the graph of a $C^1$ function, with $B$ lying on one side of each such graph. Identify the reference coordinates with the chosen initial Cartesian chart, and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Set $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$; the tensor contraction is $S:T=\sum_{i,j}S_{ij}T_{ij}$. Stress and traction have units Pa $=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

The velocity has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives, and pressure has continuous first spatial derivatives. On a compact oriented regular surface patch $S\subset\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, define its formal stress resultant to be $\int_S\sigma_En_S\,dS=-\int_Sp n_S\,dS$. A steady solution has $\partial_tu=0$. These definitions impose no boundary condition, assert no solution existence, and do not claim that the system describes an observed fluid.

These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Adopt specified scalar state laws $\mu,\zeta:\mathcal S\to[0,\infty)$ and a specified conductivity matrix law $K:\mathcal S\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, with
$$ x^T\operatorname{sym}K(\xi)x\ge0\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad \operatorname{sym}K:=(K+K^T)/2. $$
The conductivity law is tensor-valued and may be anisotropic; no restriction $K=kI_3$ is imposed. Define $\operatorname{Sym}(3):=\{D\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:D^T=D\}$ and $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. At a fixed state, let $\mathcal A_\xi:\operatorname{Sym}(3)\to\operatorname{Sym}(3)$ assign the viscous stress to the symmetric rate matrix. Here $p$ is the scalar pressure field in the tension-positive convention: the traction on an outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Under a rigid observer rotation $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$, tensor fields transform by $S^*=QSQ^T$; $\mu,\zeta$ are scalar state functions and $K^*=QKQ^T$. The viscous response is isotropic in this proper-rotation sense, while the conductivity tensor transforms covariantly and may be anisotropic. The mathematical linear-isotropic classification identifies this stress form from the stated domain, codomain, linearity and equivariance hypotheses; it does not establish that any material adopts them.

In SI units, $D,\theta,D_0$ are in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\mu,\zeta$ in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $K$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, $q$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\sigma,\tau,p$ in $\mathrm{Pa}$. If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ open. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation is $\oint_\gamma u\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable is $\int_S u\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction on $S$ is $\sigma n_S$ and the formal resultant force is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma n_S\,dS$. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\in I$ and $x\in\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$, where $s$ is a curve parameter, not time. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\infty|\to0$ in the scalar case and $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\to\infty$.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\rho_0,\mu,P,V,\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.

Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. All volume integrals here use the componentwise Riemann integral by zero extension to a containing closed rectangle. A bounded set is Jordan measurable when its indicator has such a Riemann integral; a set has content zero when, for every positive $\varepsilon$, it has a finite cover by axis-parallel boxes whose total volume is less than $\varepsilon$, where box volume is the product of side lengths. For each permitted $V$ and its image $\chi_t(V)$, their compact closures are Jordan measurable and their boundaries have content zero. For every continuous scalar integrand $f$ on a neighborhood of $\chi_t(\overline V)$, $\int_{\chi_t(V)}f\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(\overline V)}f\,dx$; the analogous equality is used on $V$ and $\overline V$. Vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise. These are the earlier $C^1$-region integral conventions, so the displayed balances over open material regions have the same meaning as their compact-closure transport formulas. For each current boundary $S=\partial\chi_t(V)$, surface integration is the finite-chart Riemann convention: for any continuous scalar $f$ on $S$, choose regular $C^1$ graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ and a finite nonnegative subordinate smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with compact support in the chart neighborhoods and sum one on $S$, and put $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{U_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))}\,dy$. Each parameter integrand is extended by zero outside $U_j$. These integrals are finite and independent of charts and partition; in graph coordinates the density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The unit normal is the continuous outward normal, and vector surface integrals are componentwise. Thus all traction, work, heat and entropy fluxes below use the same boundary-area convention. When a consuming mathematical theorem separately assumes Countable Choice, these continuous-field surface integrals also agree with its finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density; that conditional mathematical agreement adds no choice assumption to this physical postulate. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. For the weak formulation, adopt Countable Choice (every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function) and the restricted Euclidean Lebesgue spaces, almost-everywhere equality and integral conventions of the conservative weak-form definition. These conventions concern the weak initial data. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

If the same stress is written $2\mu D+\lambda\theta I_3$, then $\lambda=\zeta-2\mu/3$; no nonnegativity of $\lambda$ is assumed. These specified constitutive functions are adopted model inputs, not measured coefficient values or consequences of balance laws.

Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open time interval and $\Omega\subset I\times\mathbb R^3$ open. $$ \rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}\sigma, $$

On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. At each thermal boundary patch, select and state compatible data of one of these forms: insulation, $q\cdot n=0$; prescribed temperature, $T=T_b$ for a specified field $T_b>0$ in kelvins; or prescribed outward conductive heat flux, $q\cdot n=q_b$ for a specified field $q_b$ in watts per square metre. These are alternative boundary models. Their energy and entropy fluxes are accounted for through the chosen boundary data; no separate surface storage or reservoir entropy law is implicit.

A periodic cell with side lengths $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ metres is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z)$. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. Paired fluxes then cancel in cell integrals. These identified faces are not physical walls.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, prescribe only the fields present in the selected model. Require them to satisfy the exact function-space regularity, positivity, differential constraints, constitutive state-domain restrictions, and wall or periodic compatibility hypotheses of the particular evolution result being used. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval measured in seconds and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ an open spatial region measured in metres in a Newtonian Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0>0$ be constant in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u\in C^2(I\times\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $p\in C^1(I\times\Omega)$ pressure in pascals. Define $(\operatorname{div}u)=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$ and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The selected unforced incompressible Euler branch is
$$\rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=0.$$
Here $p$ is a constraint multiplier. No viscous stress or equation of state is included. Initial, wall, periodic and other boundary data are separate inputs. This is an adopted model formulation, not a derivation of empirical validity or an assertion of solution existence.

Let $a,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, and on $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$ define $n=x/r$, $\phi(x)=(U\cdot x)(1+a^3/(2r^3))$, $u=\nabla\phi$, and $p=p_\infty+\rho_0(|U|^2-|u|^2)/2$. Then $u,p$ are smooth in the exterior and up to $r=a$, $u\to U$ and $p\to p_\infty$ uniformly in direction at infinity, and $u\cdot n=0$ on $r=a$. The pair solves $(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the steady formal constant-density incompressible Euler system. Its boundary condition is impermeable slip/no-through: $u$ is generally nonzero tangent to the sphere, so this is not a no-slip solution. For the formal Euler stress $\sigma_E=-pI_3$ and sphere normal $n=x/a$ pointing from the center into the exterior, the exact resultant is

$$\int_{|x|=a}\sigma_E n\,dS=-\int_{|x|=a}p n\,dS=0.$$

The theorem concerns only this explicit inviscid mathematical model; it asserts neither a viscous zero-drag result nor an observed force. Under SI interpretation, $a,r,x$ are in metres, $U,u$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, and $p,p_\infty$ in pascals.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation is $\oint_\gamma u\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable is $\int_S u\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction on $S$ is $\sigma n_S$ and the formal resultant force is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma n_S\,dS$. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\in I$ and $x\in\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$, where $s$ is a curve parameter, not time. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\infty|\to0$ in the scalar case and $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\to\infty$.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\rho_0,\mu,P,V,\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.

before.quote: > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. after.quote: Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $u,v\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $f$ and $g$ be integrable between $u$ and $v$.
If $\eta\ge0$ and

$$|f(x)-g(x)|\le\eta$$

throughout the closed interval with endpoints $u$ and $v$, then

$$\left|\int_u^v f-\int_u^v g\right|\le \eta\,|v-u|.$$

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

before.claim: Fix an admissible reference region V and t0 in I, and put K=V-bar. Its C1 boundary makes K a compact Jordan set. Apply the material-transport identity in F5, componentwise to q=rho u, on a relatively compact neighborhood of K and a time-translated interval containing 0 at t0. Because rho is constant and div u=0, D_t(rho u)+(rho u) div u=rho(partial_t u+(u dot grad)u). The open-region integral compatibility in F5 identifies the resulting compact-Jordan integrals with those over chi_t(V), giving the displayed derivative.

By F5, chi_t(V) is a bounded C1 domain and its open-region integral agrees with the compact-Jordan integral. The adopted Newtonian stress [F3] is C1 up to its boundary by the stated field regularity, since the image closure is compactly contained in Omega_t. Apply [F4] to each row of sigma to replace its traction resultant by the integral of div sigma. Substitution of step 1.1 into [A1] gives zero integral of the continuous residual R on every such V; the hypotheses of [F4] hold by the stated regularity, C2 motion and [A2].

Fix t and x0 in Omega_t. For sufficiently small r, the closed ball lies in Omega_t. Apply F5 to the inverse diffeomorphism chi_t^{-1} on a neighborhood of this ball; its inverse image V is bounded, has C1 boundary and compact closure in B. Step 2.1 gives zero integral of R over the ball. Continuity rules out a positive or negative value of any component at x0, so R=0 throughout Omega_t.

after.claim: Fix an admissible reference region $V$ and a time $t_0\in I$, and put $K=\overline V$. Its $C^1$ boundary makes $K$ a compact Jordan set. Apply the material-transport identity in [F5], componentwise to $q=\rho u$, on a relatively compact neighborhood of $K$ and a time-translated interval containing $0$ at $t_0$. Because $\rho$ is constant and $\operatorname{div}u=0$, $D_t(\rho u)+(\rho u)\operatorname{div}u=\rho(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u)$. The open-region integral compatibility in [F5] identifies the resulting compact-Jordan integrals with those over $\chi_t(V)$, so $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u)\,dx$ at $t=t_0$.

By [F5], the image $\chi_t(V)$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain. The adopted Newtonian stress [F3] is $C^1$ up to its boundary by the stated field regularity, since $\overline{\chi_t(V)}$ is compactly contained in $\Omega_t$. Apply [F4] to each row of $\sigma$ to replace its traction resultant by $\int_{\chi_t(V)}\operatorname{div}\sigma\,dx$. Substitution of step 1.1 into [A1] gives $\int_{\chi_t(V)}R(t,x)\,dx=0$ for every such $V$, where $R:=\rho(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u)-\rho b-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ is continuous. The hypotheses of [F4] hold by the stated regularity, the $C^2$ motion and [A2].

Fix $t$ and $x_0\in\Omega_t$. For all sufficiently small $r>0$, the closed ball $\overline{B_r(x_0)}$ lies in $\Omega_t$. Apply [F5]'s $C^1$-image clause to the inverse diffeomorphism $\chi_t^{-1}$ on a neighborhood of this closed ball; then $V:=\chi_t^{-1}(B_r(x_0))$ is bounded, has $C^1$ boundary, and satisfies $\overline V\Subset B$. Step 2.1 gives $\int_{B_r(x_0)}R(t,x)\,dx=0$. If any component $R_i(t,x_0)$ were positive, continuity would make it positive on some sufficiently small ball and force its integral to be positive; if negative, the integral would be negative. Both contradict the zero integral, so $R_i(t,x_0)=0$ for each component. Thus $R=0$ throughout $\Omega_t$, which is the claimed local momentum equation.

Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Choose the positive $X_1$ axis and restrict this branch to fields depending only on absolute time $t$ and the coordinate $x:=X_1$; $u$ is the signed scalar velocity component along that axis. Here a frame means this adapted Cartesian inertial chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval of $x$ measured in metres, let $T_f>0$ be a final time measured in seconds, and take the space-time domain to be $\Omega\times(0,T_f)$. The measurable fields are mass density $\rho:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to(0,\infty)$ in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in metres per second, and specific entropy $s:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin.

Adopt a local-equilibrium constitutive chart on the open state domain $\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(v,s)$ and a $C^2$ fundamental relation $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ for specific internal energy in joules per kilogram. Let $c_v>0$ be the adopted specific-heat-at-constant-volume parameter and $R>0$ the adopted specific gas-constant parameter, each in joules per kilogram kelvin. Define the derived specific heat at constant pressure and ratio of specific heats by $c_p:=c_v+R$ and $\gamma:=c_p/c_v=1+R/c_v>1$. Choose $v_*>0$ in cubic metres per kilogram, $T_*>0$ in kelvins, and $s_*\in\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin as reference data. Adopt the calorically perfect ideal-gas relation
$$e(v,s)=c_vT_*\left(\frac{v_*}{v}\right)^{\gamma-1}\exp\left(\frac{s-s_*}{c_v}\right),$$
with the conventional additive energy reference for which the specific internal energy is zero at zero temperature. Define the thermodynamic temperature and pressure maps by $T(v,s):=\partial_s e(v,s)$ and $p(v,s):=-\partial_v e(v,s)$, holding the other state coordinate fixed. Direct differentiation gives
$$T(v,s)=\frac{e(v,s)}{c_v}>0,\qquad p(v,s)=(\gamma-1)\frac{e(v,s)}{v}>0.$$
For density and entropy coordinates define the state-pressure map $p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s):=p(1/\rho,s)$ for $\rho>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$. The spacetime state map is $v(t,x):=1/\rho(t,x)$ and $(t,x)\mapsto(v(t,x),s(t,x))\in\mathcal U$. It assigns the specific internal-energy, temperature, and thermodynamic-pressure fields by
$$e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x):=e(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad T(t,x):=(\partial_s e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x):=p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho(t,x),s(t,x))=-(\partial_v e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)).$$
Consequently $T(t,x)=e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/c_v$ and $p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x)=(\gamma-1)e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)/v(t,x)=(\gamma-1)\rho(t,x)e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)=R\rho(t,x)T(t,x)$. At fixed specific entropy $s$, the state-pressure map is proportional to $\rho^\gamma$, so $\left.\partial_\rho p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)\right|_s=\gamma p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)/\rho$; define the positive isentropic sound-speed map by $c_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s):=\sqrt{\left.\partial_\rho p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)\right|_s}=\sqrt{\gamma p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho,s)/\rho}$. This is a constant-specific-heat ideal-gas approximation, restricted to a regime where that closure is adopted.

Define momentum density $m(t,x):=\rho(t,x)u(t,x)$ in kilograms per square metre second and total energy density $E(t,x):=\rho(t,x)(e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)+u(t,x)^2/2)$ in joules per cubic metre. $$\mathcal G_\gamma=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\quad E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}>0\right\},\qquad p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right).$$
Since $\rho(t,x)>0$ and $e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x)>0$, $U(t,x)\in\mathcal G_\gamma$. For this state, $E-m^2/(2\rho)=\rho e_{\mathrm{int}}$ and $p(U(t,x))=p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x)$, so the numerical and thermodynamic pressure maps agree. $$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p(U),u(E+p(U))\right),\qquad c(U)=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma p(U)}{\rho}}.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation is $\oint_\gamma u\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable is $\int_S u\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction on $S$ is $\sigma n_S$ and the formal resultant force is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma n_S\,dS$. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\in I$ and $x\in\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$, where $s$ is a curve parameter, not time. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\infty|\to0$ in the scalar case and $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\to\infty$.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\rho_0,\mu,P,V,\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
