before.quote:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of time and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian spatial coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, with the standard right-handed orientation. A vector field $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is in the regularity class used here if $u$, its first time partial derivatives, its first spatial partial derivatives, and its second spatial partial derivatives all exist and are continuous. A pressure field is a map $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first spatial partial derivatives; a density field is a map $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ with continuous first time and first spatial partial derivatives. The scalar field $q:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ used in the rotating system below has continuous first spatial partial derivatives. A scalar function of one or several displayed real variables is $C^1$ when its first partial derivatives exist and are continuous; piecewise-$C^1$ paths have the meaning in the line-integral definition below. For a scalar field $f$, set $\nabla f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$; for a vector field $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$, set $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_{x_2}u_3-\partial_{x_3}u_2,\partial_{x_3}u_1-\partial_{x_1}u_3,\partial_{x_1}u_2-\partial_{x_2}u_1)$, and $\Delta f=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2f$, with $\Delta u$ applied componentwise. For $v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, use the right-handed cross product $v\times w=(v_2w_3-v_3w_2,v_3w_1-v_1w_3,v_1w_2-v_2w_1)$. Define the row-component Jacobian $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{i,j}$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_{j=1}^3u_j\partial_{x_j}u$.

For constants $\rho_0>0$ and $\mu>0$, define the kinematic-viscosity parameter $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. The formal constant-density incompressible Navier--Stokes system is

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Let $I_3$ denote the $3\times3$ identity matrix. The associated formal Cauchy stress matrix is $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})$. The corresponding steady Stokes system is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ together with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; it omits both the time derivative and convective term. These are definitions of pointwise mathematical systems and do not assert that a physical fluid has a solution with the stated regularity.

For a barotropic branch, meaning a pressure prescribed as a function of density alone, let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have two continuous derivatives and let $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous spatial partial derivatives through order two. The formal compressible Euler system for $u$ and positive density $\rho$ is

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

At a constant background density $\rho_0>0$ with $P'(\rho_0)>0$, the positive parameter $c$ defined by $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ is the sound-speed parameter of this mathematical branch. A separate rotating linear system, for constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R^3$ and scalar field $q$, is $\partial_tu+2\Omega\times u=-\nabla q$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$.

The vorticity field is $\operatorname{curl}u$. If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\Omega$ is a closed piecewise-$C^1$ oriented curve, with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$, its circulation is $\oint_\gamma u\cdot d\mathbf r$. If $S$ is a compact oriented regular surface patch in $\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, its volume-flux observable is $\int_S u\cdot n_S\,dS$. The traction on $S$ is $\sigma n_S$ and the formal resultant force is the componentwise surface integral $\int_S\sigma n_S\,dS$. A steady velocity field is a map $u_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ for which $u(t,x)=u_0(x)$ for all $t\in I$ and $x\in\Omega$; a streamline of $u_0$ is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u_0(x(s))$, where $s$ is a curve parameter, not time. A closed material loop on a time interval $J\subseteq I$ is a $C^1$ map $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$ and $\partial_tX(t,\theta)=u(t,X(t,\theta))$; the definition asserts no existence of such a map. For the following limit, an exterior spatial domain $\Omega$ means that there is $R_0>0$ such that $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>R_0\}\subseteq\Omega$. For a scalar or vector field $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$, respectively, and $f_\infty$ in the same target space, $f(x)\to f_\infty$ uniformly in direction as $|x|\to\infty$ means $\sup_{|e|=1}|f(re)-f_\infty|\to0$ in the scalar case and $\sup_{|e|=1}\|f(re)-f_\infty\|_2\to0$ in the vector case, with $r\to\infty$.

For one optional SI interpretation, the dimensions are $[x]=\mathrm m$, $[t]=\mathrm s$, $[u]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[\rho]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[V]=[q]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, and $[\Omega]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Thus $[\operatorname{curl}u]=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, circulation has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, volume flux has units $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, stress has units Pa, and resultant force has units N. In this interpretation $\rho_0,\mu,P,V,\Omega$ are inputs to the displayed formulas, while $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and $c^2=P'(\rho_0)$ are derived quantities relative to those formulas; this classification is not asserted to be universal across physical theories.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set of Cartesian coordinates, and fix a constant density $\rho_0>0$. Let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time derivatives, first spatial derivatives, and second spatial derivatives, and let $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ have continuous first spatial derivatives. The formal constant-density incompressible Euler system is the pointwise system

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

Use the Cartesian derivative conventions $\nabla f=(\partial_i f)_{i=1}^3$, $\operatorname{div}u=\sum_i\partial_i u_i$, and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\sum_j u_j\partial_j u$. The velocity has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives, and pressure has continuous first spatial derivatives. For this inviscid branch define the formal pressure stress by $\sigma_E=-pI_3$. On a compact oriented regular surface patch $S\subset\Omega$ with unit normal $n_S$, define its formal stress resultant to be $\int_S\sigma_En_S\,dS=-\int_Sp n_S\,dS$. A steady solution has $\partial_tu=0$. These definitions impose no boundary condition, assert no solution existence, and do not claim that the system describes an observed fluid.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Suppose $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ has continuous first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives; $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ has continuous first time and first spatial derivatives; and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is time-independent and $C^2$. Assume pointwise

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$

For any reference density $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^q P'(r)/r\,dr$ for $q>0$. For a steady velocity field, a streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval, satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$ with $u(x)$ denoting its time-independent spatial value. If $u$ and $\rho$ are independent of time, every streamline has $|u|^2/2+h(\rho)+V$ constant along it. If in addition $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component of $\Omega$, this quantity is constant throughout that component.

For any closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ satisfying $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t(t,s)=u(t,X(t,s))$, with $X_s$ and $X_{ts}$ continuous, the circulation $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$ is constant on $J$. Independently of the Euler assumptions, every $C^2$ vector field $v$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ obeys the identity

$$ (v\cdot\nabla)v=\nabla(|v|^2/2)-v\times\operatorname{curl}v. $$

No claim is made for shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative body forces, or viscous circulation. Under SI interpretation, $u$ is in metres per second, $\rho$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $P$ in pascals, and $h,V$ in square metres per second squared.

Let $T>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. A measurable function on an open Euclidean set $D$ is locally integrable if its norm has finite Lebesgue integral on every compact subset of $D$. For a space-time field on $\Omega\times[0,T)$ this condition is imposed on compact subsets in the relative topology, including those meeting $t=0$. Fields are identified when they agree almost everywhere. Let $U: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^m$, $F: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^{m\times3}$, and $S: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^m$ be such fields, and let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be locally integrable. For each row $a$, define $(\operatorname{div}_x F)_a=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}F_{aj}$ in the distributional sense, and define $F:\nabla_x\phi=\sum_{a=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^3F_{aj}\partial_{x_j}\phi_a$. The equation $\partial_tU+\operatorname{div}_xF=S$ with distributional initial datum $U_0$ means that for every $\phi\in C_c^1(\Omega\times[0,T);\mathbb R^m)$, continuously differentiable up to $t=0$ and supported away from $\partial\Omega$ and $t=T$,

$$\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\bigl(U\cdot\partial_t\phi+F:\nabla_x\phi+S\cdot\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\phi(x,0)\,dx=0.$$

No boundary condition on $\partial\Omega$ is encoded because the test fields are supported away from it. This initial identity specifies the initial datum distributionally; it does not assert $U(\cdot,t)\to U_0$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ or any other stronger trace topology. Such a trace must be assumed or proved separately. The fields are abstract mathematical variables; no physical unit system or balance postulate is imposed.

For locally integrable scalar fields $H,R,H_0$ and a locally integrable flux $Q: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^3$, the inequality $\partial_tH+\operatorname{div}_x Q\ge R$ with initial datum $H_0$ means that for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^1(\Omega\times[0,T))$ with the same support convention,

$$\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\bigl(H\,\partial_t\psi+Q\cdot\nabla_x\psi+R\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega H_0(x)\psi(x,0)\,dx\le0.$$

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\rho u\cdot\nabla\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\rho_0\phi(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Momentum balance, for every vector $\psi$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho u\cdot\partial_t\psi+(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma):\nabla\psi+\rho b\cdot\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega m_0\cdot\psi(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Total-energy balance, for every scalar $\eta$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho E\,\partial_t\eta+(\rho E u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)\cdot\nabla\eta+(\rho b\cdot u+\rho r)\eta\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\mathcal E_0\eta(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Physical entropy inequality, for every nonnegative scalar $\zeta\ge0$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho s\,\partial_t\zeta+(\rho s u+q/T)\cdot\nabla\zeta+(\rho r/T)\zeta\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega S_0\zeta(0,x)\,dx\le0.$$

Every conservative density, product, flux and source displayed in these tests is required to be locally integrable up to $t=0$, including $\rho u\otimes u$, $\rho E u$, $\sigma^{\mathsf T}u$, $q/T$ and $\rho r/T$: its absolute value has finite integral on every compact subset of $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$ in the relative topology, using its values for $t>0$. This condition assigns no point values at $t=0$ and asserts no strong initial trace. Interior test functions impose no boundary condition; walls, thermal exchange, periodic identifications and stronger initial trace conditions are separate data. This weak mass/momentum/energy adoption and the physical entropy inequality are not inferred for arbitrary discontinuous or vacuum states from the smooth balance postulate. The source term and the sign of the entropy inequality use the outward-positive heat-flux convention above.

A measurable function on an open Euclidean set $D$ is locally integrable if its norm has finite Lebesgue integral on every compact subset of $D$. on $\Gamma$. The initial-data term in the weak initial form is independent; this interior jump condition neither asserts nor requires a strong trace at $t=0$.

$$[G]\cdot n-V_n[H]\ge0$$
on $\Gamma$. These are local equivalences for prescribed piecewise-smooth fields, not existence or uniqueness theorems for nonlinear systems. The fields are abstract mathematical variables with no assigned physical units or constitutive model.

A spatial vector is an element of the Euclidean translation space; its components rotate by $Q$ under a rigid observer change. A spatial second-order tensor is a linear map from that vector space to itself, represented by a $3\times3$ matrix in a Cartesian orthonormal basis; it transforms as $S^*=QSQ^T$. A tensor-valued constitutive response is **objective** when its values at corresponding events satisfy this transformation rule for every $C^2$ rigid observer change. For a stress tensor $\sigma$, use the tension-positive convention in which the traction (force per unit current area) on a surface with outward unit normal $n$ is $\sigma n$. Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. In the continuum model used on this page, $\rho_0(a)$ is a reference mass-density field in kg m$^{-3}$, $b(t,x)$ is an adopted body-acceleration field in m s$^{-2}$, $e(t,x)$ is specific internal energy (energy per unit mass) in J kg$^{-1}=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$, $T(t,x)>0$ is temperature in K, $s(t,x)$ is specific entropy in J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$, $q(t,x)$ is heat flux (heat-transfer rate per unit area) in W m$^{-2}$, and $r(t,x)$ is specific heat supply (power per unit mass) in W kg$^{-1}$. Their adoption is a physical-model choice, not a consequence of the SI. The current mass density $\rho(t,x)$ means mass per unit current volume and has units kg m$^{-3}$; for a mass-conserving motion, its construction from $\rho_0$ and $\chi$ is established from the stated balance hypotheses in the theorem on this page. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Thus the metre, kilogram, second, and kelvin are SI base units in this dictionary, while density, velocity, acceleration, pressure, energy, power, viscosity, and heat-flux units are derived according to the BIPM SI conventions.

before.quote:
Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** supplies an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$ and the absolute-time coordinate. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ have orientation-preserving diffeomorphic time slices (bijections onto open images with $C^2$ inverses and positive Jacobian determinant), and satisfy $\chi(0,a)=a$. Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous; write $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ and $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ and $\rho\in C^1(\mathcal O)$ be positive mass densities, where $\mathcal O=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. Suppose that for every nonempty bounded open $V$ with compact closure in $B$ and $C^1$ boundary locally a graph with the region on one side and every $t\in I$,
$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$
Then the pointwise continuity equation
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)=0$$
holds throughout the balanced physical region $\mathcal O_B:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(B)\}$. The larger set $\mathcal O$ is only the ambient regularity domain; no balance outside $\chi_t(B)$ is assumed or concluded. This is a conditional deduction in the smooth material model and asserts no extension to weak fields or vacuum.

Assume countable choice. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U;\mathbb R^3)$ have orientation-preserving diffeomorphic time slices (bijections onto open images with $C^2$ inverses and positive Jacobian determinant) and satisfy $\chi(0,a)=a$, and set $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ and $\mathcal O=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$. Here $C^r$ means all coordinate partial derivatives through order $r$ are continuous. Let $\rho:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$, $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$, $e:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R$, $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$, and $\sigma:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be $C^1$ on $\mathcal O$. Let $b:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ and $r:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Their SI units are respectively kilograms per cubic metre, metres per second, joules per kilogram, watts per square metre, pascals, metres per second squared, and watts per kilogram. Put $k=|u|^2/2$, $E=e+k$, $D_xu=(\partial_{x_j}u_i)_{ij}$, $D=(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})/2$, $D_t=\partial_t+u\cdot\nabla_x$, and $A:B=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$. Use rowwise divergence $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij}$, vector divergence $\operatorname{div}q=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}q_j$, and traction $t=\sigma n$, where $n$ is the outward Euclidean unit normal and $q\cdot n>0$ denotes heat leaving the material region.

Assume pointwise mass continuity and, on every material region $P_t=\chi_t(V)$ where $V$ is a nonempty bounded open reference region with compact closure in $B$ and $C^1$ boundary locally a graph with the region on one side, the adopted linear-momentum, angular-momentum, and total-energy balances
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho u\,dx=\int_{P_t}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\sigma n\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{P_t}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}x\times(\sigma n)\,dS,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{P_t}\rho E\,dx=\int_{P_t}(\rho b\cdot u+\rho r)\,dx+\int_{\partial P_t}\bigl(u\cdot\sigma n-q\cdot n\bigr)\,dS.$$
The angular balance is about a fixed inertial origin and there are no surface couples or intrinsic spin. Then throughout the balanced physical region $\mathcal O_B:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(B)\}$, with $\mathcal O$ retained only as the ambient regularity domain,
$$\partial_t(\rho u)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma)=\rho b,$$
$$\sigma=\sigma^{\mathsf T},$$
$$\partial_t(\rho E)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho E u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)=\rho b\cdot u+\rho r,$$
and
$$\partial_t(\rho k)+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho k u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u)=\rho b\cdot u-\sigma:D,\qquad
\rho D_t e=\sigma:D-\operatorname{div}_xq+\rho r.$$
Conversely, the pointwise momentum equation and symmetric stress imply the angular-momentum balance, and the pointwise total-energy equation implies its stated material integral balance. All deductions are conditional on the smooth model and do not assert existence of a solution.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

Within a specified model, a **primitive quantity** is a quantity adopted as input rather than constructed from the other data of that model; a **derived quantity** is assigned by an explicit construction from stated inputs and results. This status is framework-local and is independent of whether its SI unit is base or derived. A pressure $p$ is a scalar in Pa whose role depends on the selected constitutive branch. The shear and bulk dynamic-viscosity parameters $\mu,\zeta$, when that branch is adopted, have units Pa s $=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$; thermal conductivity $\kappa_T$ has units W m$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. The gradient $\nabla$ has units m$^{-1}$. Work in the nonrelativistic SI fluid model on an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in seconds and oriented Euclidean three-space measured in metres. Let $\Omega_t$ be the fluid region at time $t$ and $\mathcal O:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\Omega_t\}$ its open spacetime region. Let $u:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ be fluid velocity in metres per second, $T:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $q:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^3$ conductive heat flux in watts per square metre. A moving solid boundary is covered by local material surface charts $X_b:I\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^3$, where $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is open with dimensionless labels and $X_b\in C^2(I\times\Xi;\mathbb R^3)$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives in $(t,\xi)$ of total order at most two are continuous. For each fixed $t\in I$ and each $\xi_0\in\Xi$, there is a neighborhood $V\subseteq\Xi$ of $\xi_0$ on which $X_b(t,\cdot)$ is injective, its derivative has rank two, and it is a homeomorphism onto its image; thus each time slice is locally a surface chart of the wall. These charts carry fixed material labels: wherever two such charts overlap, their labels are related by a time-independent $C^2$ coordinate change $\varphi$, so that $X_b^i(t,\xi)=X_b^j(t,\varphi(\xi))$ on the overlap. Differentiation in $t$ then gives the same velocity at each represented boundary point, and $w_b$ is the well-defined material boundary velocity $w_b(t,X_b(t,\xi)):=\partial_tX_b(t,\xi)$ in metres per second. For each $t$, every represented wall patch $X_b(t,\Xi)$ lies in $\partial\Omega_t$; locally this boundary is a $C^2$ graph with $\Omega_t$ on one side. Define $\Gamma_b:=\{(t,X_b(t,\xi)):t\in I,\ \xi\in\Xi\}$, taking the union over wall charts. The unit normal $n:\Gamma_b\to\mathbb R^3$ points outward from the fluid region $\Omega_t$ into the solid and is continuous. In the smooth branch, assume $u,T,q$ have continuous traces wherever boundary values are imposed. The no-penetration or impermeability condition is the adopted equality $(u-w_b)\cdot n=0$ on the wall. When separately selected, no-slip is the stronger adopted equality $u=w_b$ on the wall. Neither equality is deduced from an interior balance equation; no-slip is not part of the inviscid wall model unless explicitly adopted.

On a thermal patch $\Gamma_T\subseteq\Gamma_b$, a prescribed temperature is a map $T_b:\Gamma_T\to(0,\infty)$ and a prescribed outward heat flux is a map $q_b:\Gamma_T\to\mathbb R$. Require their pullbacks $(t,\xi)\mapsto T_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$ and $(t,\xi)\mapsto q_b(t,X_b(t,\xi))$, wherever selected, to be continuous, with any additional regularity required by the chosen evolution problem stated separately. Periodicity identifies opposite faces by the corresponding translations and requires equality of the fields and of each derivative trace required by the selected evolution problem. These conventions concern the weak initial data. In the weak formulation, initial data enter through the test-function initial term; that fixes a distributional initial datum but does not by itself supply a strong trace. This postulate selects model data only. It asserts no existence, uniqueness, regularity improvement, approximation, or solvability for any initial-boundary value problem.

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference region with $C^1$ boundary (locally a $C^1$ graph with the region on one side), and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open neighborhood of $\overline B$.
